body: What it is: a State leadership development program for employees, administered by Minnesota Management and Budget.

Why it is here: leadership pathways should connect to programs that exist. Correcting the record matters; an earlier draft described a DHS-owned Emerging Leaders program that public evidence does not support.

How to use it: check eligibility, timing, and the nomination process at the source. Supervisors can use sponsorship to make sure people from underrepresented communities know about it and are nominated.

body: Transitions to plan for: nomination and application, interview or selection event, acting or stretch assignment, leadership cohort or program, new team or new supervisor, and return from leave.
For each transition, name one owner responsible for carrying existing accommodations forward and for offering accommodation to everyone entering it. The owner is a person, not a process.
Carry the accommodation, not the diagnosis. The receiving supervisor or program needs to know what works, not why. The accommodation process holds the confidential record.
Offer accommodation to everyone at every transition, in the same sentence used for logistics, so no one has to disclose to receive it.
Design cohort events accessible by default: materials in advance, captioning, flexible participation formats, no timed or drag-based activities, and time to rest.
Check after the transition. Ask everyone, not only people who requested something, whether the arrangements worked, and fix what did not.
Boundaries. Accommodation decisions and disputes belong to Human Resources and the accommodation process. This aid is about pathway design and ownership; it does not decide any accommodation.
publishedOriginal.title: Accommodations across transitions: closing the accommodation cliff
publishedOriginal.summary: Accommodations that work in the current role are often lost during a rotation, an acting assignment, a leadership cohort, or an interview process because nobody owns them across the transition. This aid names the transitions, the owner for each, and what to carry.
publishedOriginal.provenance: Drafted September 5, 2026 from the reconstruction decision baseline and the content recovery report; owner item-level review recorded in the domain release manifest.
publishedOriginal.whyItMatters: The cliff is invisible to the people who design pathways and very visible to the people who fall off it. Naming an owner for accommodations across each transition is a small change that removes a structural barrier.

body: Policy: Which laws, rules, rights, and required safeguards apply? Who benefits, who carries added work or risk, and whose needs are missing? Which rules or routine practices shape the result? What can your team change, and what must be reviewed by the person with authority to decide?

Budget: Which costs cover interpreting, translation, accessible formats, and payment for community partners? Which costs have been treated as free? If funding is reduced, whose services would be affected first?

Technology: Are accessibility requirements written into the specifications and tested by people who use assistive technology? What information is collected? Could it be used to sort, rank, or profile people?

Procurement: Do the selection criteria give real weight to accessibility, language access, and community knowledge? Do the requirements create unnecessary barriers for small providers or community organizations?
publishedOriginal.title: Equity impact questions for policy, budget, technology, and procurement
publishedOriginal.summary: Use this short question set for high-stakes decisions. Consider which authority and rights apply, who benefits, who carries the burden, which assumptions shape the outcome, what can change, and what must stay with the responsible official.

body: Keep the session connected to practice: limit presentation time so participants can spend at least half the session working with the ideas themselves.
Bring real work: ask participants to bring a notice, a plan, or a meeting they own. Practice on that.
Facilitator role: participants know their own programs. Your role is to offer useful questions, guide the conversation, and keep the group on time.

Access: ask in advance what participants need. Arrange captions, spoken-language or sign-language interpretation, translated or accessible materials, and alternatives to dragging or timed activities. Build access into the session from the beginning.
Follow-up: schedule a short check-in to learn whether participants were able to use what they completed.
publishedOriginal.title: Facilitation that participants can use in their work
publishedOriginal.summary: A useful session helps participants make a meaningful change in their own work. Begin with what they should leave able to do, keep presentations focused, and give them substantial time to practice with real materials.

body: Where power sits. Role, tenure, credential, language fluency, familiarity with the organization, race, disability, and who the process was designed for all shape who is heard.
What it does. People with less power wait to be asked, soften disagreement, and stop offering ideas that were ignored once. People with more power mistake that quiet for agreement.
What to do with it. Speak last. Ask the newest and the quietest first. Credit ideas to the person who had them. Change the format so contribution does not depend on speaking fast in English.
In supervision. Ask what the person needs from you rather than telling them what you need. Make expectations explicit so people do not have to guess the unwritten rules.

Across difference. Cultural humility means assuming you do not know how your habits land and asking. The Intercultural Development Inventory can help a person see their own orientation; it is one tool, used by qualified administrators, and never a label or a rating.
publishedOriginal.title: Positional power: seeing it, naming it, and using it well
publishedOriginal.summary: Supervisors, managers, and people with expertise or tenure hold power that shapes who speaks, who is believed, and whose time counts. Seeing it is the first intercultural skill; using it deliberately is the second.
publishedOriginal.provenance: Drafted September 5, 2026 from the reconstruction decision baseline and the content recovery report; owner item-level review recorded in the domain release manifest.

body: Engagement without forced disclosure. Work through anonymous aggregate listening, disability employee resource groups, and trusted intermediaries, with small-group suppression in any reporting. Ask about the pathway, not the person: what does it take to be seen as ready for a lead role here, who explains it, and what happens when someone asks for an accommodation during a stretch assignment or interview.
Close the loop publicly. Disabled staff in particular have watched accessibility promises go unfunded. Report what changed, what did not, and who owns the next step.

Examine the pipeline stage by stage: nomination to leadership programs, selection for visible projects, acting assignments, interview formats, and promotion outcomes. Disability is often absent from disaggregated workforce data, so the first finding may be that the organization cannot see the pattern at all. Say so.

Test the job-relatedness of leadership criteria. Executive presence, quick verbal response, travel, long hours, and always-on availability screen out many disabled staff and are rarely tied to what leaders actually do.

Look for the accommodation cliff. Accommodations that exist for the current role are often lost during a rotation, a leadership cohort, or an interview process because nobody owns them across the transition. Name an owner for accommodations across every transition.

Sponsorship, not just mentoring. Mentoring gives advice; sponsorship puts someone's name forward. Pair disabled staff who want it with sponsors who hold decision power, and track at the program level whether sponsorship leads to assignments.
Reverse mentoring, where disabled staff advise leaders on what accessible leadership looks like, with compensation or recognized time and never as a standing expectation.

Accessible leadership programs by default: materials in advance, captioning, flexible participation formats, no timed or drag-based activities, and accommodations carried across every cohort event. The State of Minnesota Emerging Leaders Institute run by Minnesota Management and Budget is the verified public program; DHS-level pathways should be reviewed against the same standard.
Transparent pathway maps that say what a lead or supervisor role requires, which experiences count, and how to get them, so advancement does not depend on informal networks.
Structured leadership interviews with rubrics tied to the work, accommodations offered without asking why, and panel preparation on disability bias.
Stay conversations that ask about growth and access together, and exit patterns reviewed at an appropriate level.

Boundaries this program keeps. No guessing about disability: the program never guesses who is disabled from behavior, accommodation history, or participation. No individual tracking: private learning and reflection stay private, and program-level measures use aggregates with suppression. Accommodation requests, complaints, and personnel decisions go to the confidential channels, never into this program.
Who owns what. ADA and accommodation decisions belong to Human Resources and the accommodation process. Pathway design belongs to leadership and the equity practice. Take each to its owner.
publishedOriginal.title: Accessible leadership pathways and sponsorship for staff with disabilities
publishedOriginal.summary: For staff with disabilities, advancement barriers are usually structural and often invisible to the people who run leadership pathways. This note adapts the engagement, analysis, and applied-practice sequence to that reality: hear from disabled staff without forcing disclosure, examine the pipeline stage by stage, and build sponsorship, transparent pathway maps, and accessible leadership programs by default.

body: What the IDI is. A licensed intercultural assessment administered by qualified administrators. It describes a developmental orientation toward cultural difference and is used for individual and group development.

What it is not. It is not a measure of competence for selection, promotion, or performance. A result or an inferred orientation must never become an employee record, an access gate, or a hidden label in this program.
What this program does with it. Describes it, names its owner and license, and routes people to qualified administration if their division offers it. Protected content is not reproduced.

The same discipline applies to every tool. The Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit, the GARE Racial Equity Toolkit, CLAS, LifeCourse, implicit-association resources, accessibility methods, and engagement frameworks each have an owner, an evidence base, a license or public status, required qualifications, limits, and permitted uses. The tool cards in the Library record them.
Practical application is decided through the consultant-led, equity-professional-informed practice, in collaboration with Equity Directors, Specialists, and committee members. No tool decides it.
publishedOriginal.title: The IDI and other tools: inputs to practice, not the practice itself
publishedOriginal.summary: The Intercultural Development Inventory is one proprietary assessment among many tools. It can inform qualified professional practice. It does not define this program, its results are never personnel data, and its protected content is not reproduced here.
publishedOriginal.provenance: Drafted September 5, 2026 from the reconstruction decision baseline and the content recovery report; owner item-level review recorded in the domain release manifest.
publishedOriginal.whyItMatters: A single instrument can quietly become the program's definition of competence. That is a governance risk. A registry of tools with owners, evidence, limits, and permitted uses keeps every tool in its place.

body: Start with the available resources: search Resources, open a relevant community brief, or use a checklist. These options may give you what you need without a meeting.

Employee Culture, Human Resources, civil rights, or accommodation: use the appropriate established process for a complaint, investigation, grievance, discipline matter, or accommodation decision about a named person. Keep names and case details out of this program.

Policy or legal owner: contact this person when two sources conflict, a statute or rule needs interpretation, or no official source is available. If you cannot confirm the source, say that clearly and ask the policy or legal owner. Do not create or quote a citation from memory.
Office of Indian Policy or Tribal liaison: any work touching a Tribal Nation, Native children, Tribal data, services, or land. Consultation is government-to-government and comes first.
Equity Director: contact the Equity Director for questions about an administration's pilot, local guidance, or proposed content.

Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant: consider a consultation when an early program idea or high-stakes decision needs another perspective. A consultation may also help when available guidance does not fully address community-specific work. Go to Support to request a consultation or first review what information you would share. A meeting is optional.
publishedOriginal.title: When to seek additional guidance, and where to begin
publishedOriginal.summary: Many questions can be answered with a checklist, job aid, or other resource. Use the established Employee Culture, Human Resources, civil-rights, or accommodation process for complaints, investigations, discipline, and accommodation decisions. Ask the policy or legal owner when official guidance conflicts or is missing. If the work may affect a Tribal Nation, contact the Office of Indian Policy or designated Tribal liaison before planning engagement. A consultation may help with a new program idea, a high-stakes decision, or a community question that remains unresolved.
